tidle.intro: I built Tidle to make everyday tasks easier to keep in view. Quick capture, categories, and subtasks keep plans organized, while reminders and recurring tasks help the day stay on track.
tidle.widgetLabel: Tidle Today's Tasks widget: Done 0 of 8
tidle.demo: Today's progress, at a glance. Drag to explore.
tidle.widgetsBody: Home Screen and Lock Screen widgets show completed tasks at a glance, with shortcuts to Today and task creation.
tidle.stepsBody: Break larger tasks into smaller steps. Schedule a reminder or repeat a task on chosen days.
tidle.routineBody: A focused task list keeps the interface clear. Completion analytics help reveal weekly patterns and support a steady routine.

survey.label: 58 percent of users with prior sewing experience said finding time for sewing was a challenge: 11 of 19 respondents. Each bubble is one respondent: 11 navy bubbles selected this difficulty and eight pale blue bubbles did not. Multiple choices were allowed. Exploratory survey, October 2026, recruited through word of mouth and social channels.

restitch.intro: Small sewing projects, broken into visual steps. Restitch helps you hem a pair of jeans or make a fabric flower, using what you have and moving at your own pace.
restitch.sampleBody: 36 people responded through word of mouth and social channels. Of the 33 who reported their age, 4 were 18–24 and 29 were 25–34; 3 did not provide an age.
restitch.sampleLimits: The time finding uses 19 answers from people who had sewn before. All were aged 18–34, with 17 aged 25–34. Multiple choices were allowed. This exploratory sample is concentrated in ages 25–34 and describes reported difficulties, rather than measured use of Restitch.
restitch.makeBody: Two projects to start with: a clean double-fold hem for your jeans, or a hand-sewn faux-leather flower made from six petals and a button.
restitch.stepsBody: Each project begins with a materials checklist, followed by six visual lessons. Jeans lessons include short animations you can pause, scrub, and replay; the flower uses step-by-step photographs.
restitch.progressTitle: Pick up where you left off
restitch.progressBody: Materials readiness and completed steps stay saved in your browser. Return to an earlier lesson or continue a project at your own pace.

fuzz.title: Breadboard fuzz.
fuzz.intro: I built a fuzz circuit on a breadboard and tested its output through a guitar amp. This is the working setup, with its wires, components, and sound out in the open.

MPSA14 transistor, BAT41 collector-to-base diode, 10 kilohm collector resistor, 470 nanofarad input capacitor, 100 nanofarad output capacitor, and 100 kilohm volume potentiometer. These reference values and connections have not been verified against the photographed breadboard.

thinkingCap.title: Thinking cap.
thinkingCap.intro: An old sweater, turned into a fitted beanie. My plan for making one, following wynunlimited’s tutorial.
thinkingCap.step1: Print the PDF at 100% / Actual size on A4 or Letter. Check the 50 mm square, then choose a size from the head measurements. Try a test first: knits stretch differently.
thinkingCap.step2: Use an old knit sweater, or about ¼ metre of 60-inch-wide knit. Cut four pieces on the fold, with the stretch running across the head. Snip tiny 2 mm notches at both ends of each fold.
thinkingCap.step3: Pair the pieces, right sides together. Match the tips and centre notches; sew one curved side of each pair at ¼ in (6 mm). Backstitch both ends. Sew slowly without stretching; the tutorial uses a 2.5 mm stitch. Press the seams open to reduce bulk.
thinkingCap.step4: Open both pairs and place them right sides together. Match the seams and side notches, then pin around the edge. Leave a 2 in / 5 cm turning gap near the inside crown. Sew the rest of the perimeter at ¼ in, backstitching at the gap.
thinkingCap.step5: Turn through the gap and stitch it closed. Tuck that half inside the other, matching the crown seams. Gently press the bottom fold. Optional: hand-tack the two crowns together so the layers stay put in the wash.
thinkingCap.tackCaption: a small stitch through both crowns
thinkingCap.heroAlt: The tutorial’s finished four-panel beanie held over an ironing board, shown in black and white.
thinkingCap.scaleAlt: The pattern cover’s square marked 2 inches or 5 centimetres for checking the print scale.
thinkingCap.patternAlt: The size 3 pattern showing cut four, a horizontal stretch arrow, cut on fold, and quarter-inch seam allowance.
thinkingCap.cutAlt: Four knit pieces opened out, with pointed ends and centre folds, shown in black and white.
thinkingCap.pinAlt: Two pairs of knit panels with one curved side pinned on each pair.
thinkingCap.pressAlt: The two sewn pairs opened out, with their seam allowances pressed apart.
thinkingCap.gapAlt: The joined panels pinned around the perimeter, with the small turning gap indicated near a crown.
thinkingCap.turnAlt: The right-side-out double-ended beanie before one half is tucked inside the other.
thinkingCap.tackAlt: A hand-sewing needle joining the inner and outer crown at their seam intersections.
thinkingCap.credit: Reference frames from wynunlimited’s tutorial. Click a picture to enlarge, or its time to rewatch.
thinkingCap.borderNote: For the bottom edge, I’d add cream barbed-wire stitching 2 cm above the fold. Work on the outer halves while flat: two close rows, dense little wraps, then Xs beside each wrap. Match the pattern across seams, keep the lining free, and test the stretch first.
thinkingCap.borderAlt: The Instagram tutorial showing dense thread wraps and crossed barbs along two rows of stitching.
thinkingCap.previewCaption: the planned finish · drag to turn
thinkingCap.previewAlt: A charcoal four-panel knit cap with a cream barbed-wire stitch circling its lower edge. Drag or use the arrow keys to turn it.
